article_title: Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal
citation: Pynoo, B., Tondeur, J., Van Braak, J., Duyck, W., Sijnave, B. & Duyck, P. (2012). Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1308-1317. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.026
title: C-TAM-TPB: Combined Technology Acceptance Model and Theory of Planned Behavior
description: The C-TAM-TPB framework combines the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) to explain technology acceptance through five determinants: perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and attitude. These predict behavioral intention, which in turn predicts self-reported frequency of use and observed use. The article states that "This combined model incorporates the five determinants" and applies it per user type to explain portal acceptance among teachers.
requirements: Questionnaire measurement of all five determinants plus behavioral intention and self-reported frequency of use
constraints: Developed for voluntary-use settings; the article notes that findings may differ from business settings because educational institutions serve different goals and teachers have autonomy in technology choice
target_learners: Teachers in primary and secondary education
target_learning_goals: Understanding and predicting teachers' acceptance and use of educational technology
examples: Applied to explain KlasCement portal acceptance among 919 Flemish and Dutch teachers
key_sources: Pynoo, B., Tondeur, J., Van Braak, J., Duyck, W., Sijnave, B. & Duyck, P. (2012). Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1308-1317. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.026

article_title: Evaluating the evaluators: does C-SATS measure up?
citation: Laverty Robert B., Chesnut Charles H., Karam Joseph R., L'Huillier Joseph C., Bonte Alexander, Clanahan Julie M., Park Jisuk, Yoon Brian, Krell Robert W. (2025). Evaluating the evaluators: does C-SATS measure up? Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-025-12150-0
title: C-SATS crowd-sourced video assessment platform with GEARS rubric
description: C-SATS is a commercial, Seattle-based platform that acquires secure operating-room video and performs blinded skill assessments using the Global Evaluative Assessment of Robotic Skills (GEARS) rubric, which "assesses 6 separate domains—depth perception, bimanual dexterity, efficiency, autonomy, force sensitivity, and robotic control" on a 5-point scale with performance anchors at 1, 3, and 5, averaged across evaluators. Its methodology of training non-expert medical personnel as reviewers has been validated in other settings. In this study it was used to score 70 RAC and RIHR videos from 48 surgeons.
requirements: Blinded reviewers not known to participating surgeons, and reviewer training in the GEARS methodology
constraints: The platform could not disclose its inter-rater reliability data, reporting only that all values were greater than 0.9
target_learning_goals: Assessment of robotic surgical technical skill and proficiency for training and credentialing
examples: 48 surgeons submitted 70 videos of RAC and/or RIHR for blinded GEARS review on the platform
key_sources: Laverty Robert B., Chesnut Charles H., Karam Joseph R., L'Huillier Joseph C., Bonte Alexander, Clanahan Julie M., Park Jisuk, Yoon Brian, Krell Robert W. (2025). Evaluating the evaluators: does C-SATS measure up? Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-025-12150-0

article_title: Emergent Explicit Regulation in College Students Collaborative Scientific Inquiry Learning, Framework and A Case Study
citation: Ying Cao, Tong Wan, Andrew Burns, Ethan Cusack, and Pierre-Philippe A. Ouimet. (2025). Emergent Explicit Regulation in College Students' Collaborative Scientific Inquiry Learning—Framework and A Case Study. https://www.rit.edu
title: C-Inquiry: a characterization of collaborative inquiry learning combining inquiry practices, authenticity, collaboration, and content knowledge
description: The authors adapt Vauras et al.'s three core aspects of science learning—authenticity, collaboration, and inquiry—into a comprehensive characterization called C-Inquiry. Inquiry practices are elaborated primarily with the NGSS's eight science practices, plus an added practice zero (orientation) from Pedaste et al.'s phases, and 'conceptualization' replacing 'asking questions'. Authenticity, collaboration, and content knowledge permeate all inquiry practices, and EER instances can be situated within this framework.
requirements: Situating EER instances within inquiry practices requires activity designs that map onto the NGSS practices and Pedaste phases
constraints: The framework separates inquiry practice from content knowledge, aligning with NGSS strands; developed for collaborative science inquiry contexts
target_learners: college students in inquiry-based science programs
target_learning_goals: engaging in scientific inquiry practices such as developing models and investigating
examples: Brittany's EER was situated in inquiry practice 2: developing a model
key_sources: Ying Cao, Tong Wan, Andrew Burns, Ethan Cusack, and Pierre-Philippe A. Ouimet. (2025). Emergent Explicit Regulation in College Students' Collaborative Scientific Inquiry Learning—Framework and A Case Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.09923

article_title: Psychometric evaluation of the Indonesian version of the confidence scale among primary healthcare nurses in dengue-related prevention practice.
citation: Hertanti Nuzul Sri, Nguyen Nga Thi Thuy, Chi Do Thi Kim, Chuang Yeu-Hui. (2026). Psychometric evaluation of the Indonesian version of the confidence scale among primary healthcare nurses in dengue-related prevention practice. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09471-6
title: C-Scale-I: a five-item Indonesian Confidence Scale for dengue-related prevention practice
description: The C-Scale-I is a cross-culturally adapted Indonesian version of Grundy's five-item Confidence Scale, measuring nurses' perceived confidence in dengue-related prevention practice. Each item is rated on a five-point Likert scale, with total scores from 5 to 25 where "higher scores indicating greater confidence." Items cover certainty of performance, absence of hesitation, perceived competence, and satisfaction. Its brevity makes it practical for nurses with demanding workloads.
requirements: Permission from the original developer and a six-step cross-cultural adaptation process (forward translation, synthesis, backward translation, expert review, pretesting, appraisal) were used to establish conceptual and semantic comparability
constraints: Validated specifically among PHC nurses in Indonesia in the context of dengue-related prevention practice; applicability to other populations and settings should be examined
target_learners: Primary healthcare nurses in dengue-endemic settings
target_learning_goals: Assessing perceived confidence in performing dengue-related prevention practice
examples: Items were contextualized by adding "dengue infection prevention practice" after the term "performance" and expanding "observer" to patients, families, community members, and colleagues
key_sources: Hertanti Nuzul Sri, Nguyen Nga Thi Thuy, Chi Do Thi Kim, Chuang Yeu-Hui. (2026). Psychometric evaluation of the Indonesian version of the confidence scale among primary healthcare nurses in dengue-related prevention practice. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09471-6

article_title: Sequential learning of psychomotor and visuospatial skills for laparoscopic suturing and knot tying - study protocol for a randomized controlled trial "The shoebox study".
citation: Hendrie JD, Nickel F, Bruckner T, Kowalewski K-F, Garrow CR, Mantel M, Romero P, Müller-Stich BP. (2016). Sequential learning of psychomotor and visuospatial skills for laparoscopic suturing and knot tying – study protocol for a randomized controlled trial “The shoebox study”. Trials 17. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13063-015-1145-8
title: C-loop proficiency criteria: a 23-point procedural checklist, a 5-point knot quality scale, and a competency table
description: The protocol defines proficiency with three instruments: a previously validated modified 23-point procedural implementation checklist originally published by Munz et al., a 5-point knot quality scale by Muresan et al. assessing throws, tightness, edge opposition and tension, and a competency table setting goals. The protocol states a trainee demonstrates competency "upon finishing it in ≤01:15 (min:sec), attaining ≥18 points on the procedural implementation checklist, scoring ≥4 on the knot quality scale, and maintaining stitching ≤2 mm" from the pad's entry and exit points.
requirements: Trained peer tutors to provide expert assessment once a training partner judges competency reached
constraints: Proficiency requires completing the C-loop on two consecutive occasions meeting the criteria, once with the partner and once with the peer tutor
target_learners: medical students training in laparoscopic suturing
target_learning_goals: standardized assessment of procedural competency and knot quality
examples: Accuracy is recorded by measuring the distance in mm of the stitch from the edge of the entry and exit points of the standardized suture pad
key_sources: Hendrie JD, Nickel F, Bruckner T, Kowalewski K-F, Garrow CR, Mantel M, Romero P, Müller-Stich BP. (2016). Sequential learning of psychomotor and visuospatial skills for laparoscopic suturing and knot tying – study protocol for a randomized controlled trial “The shoebox study”. Trials 17. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13063-015-1145-8
